item.title: Ken Paxton’s State-Funded Jet-Setting Draws Campaign Scrutiny
item.description:
Where in the world is Ken Paxton?

In 2021, Mr. Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, and his wife left town for Utah during a deadly winter storm that left millions in his home state without power. When lawyers tried to depose him in a securities-fraud case in 2023, he was roving around Europe. And this past summer, in the middle of his hotly contested U.S. Senate campaign, a British tabloid spotted Mr. Paxton in Iceland and London.

Since his 2015 swearing-in as the state’s top lawyer, Mr. Paxton has taken about 350 trips outside Texas with a taxpayer-funded security detail, including 25 to foreign countries such as South Africa, India and Aruba, according to a New York Times analysis of data from the Texas Department of Public Safety. Texas law does not limit Mr. Paxton’s use of state-sponsored protection to official business.

Mr. Paxton also has benefited from the largess of wealthy friends, who donated $730,000 toward his legal bills in the securities-fraud case and have treated him to hunting and fishing trips, airplane flights and lodging, and tickets to various events, including the Grammy Awards, records show.

Mr. Paxton’s Democratic rival, James Talarico, has sought to turn the attorney general’s lifestyle into a liability, repeatedly accusing him of exploiting the perks of his office to enrich himself. Mr. Talarico, a state representative, has dinged Mr. Paxton on his apparent affinity for luxuries big and small — from his real estate portfolio that includes at least 15 properties worth about $9 million to the $1,000 pen he once swiped from a courthouse security tray. Polls indicate a tight race in a conservative state that hasn’t elected a Democrat in more than three decades, suggesting that Mr. Talarico’s attacks may be resonating with some voters.

“He became a multimillionaire on a government salary,” Mr. Talarico said in a widely viewed social media post. “He takes lavish vacations in Iceland while Texans can’t afford the basics. Ken Paxton doesn’t serve us — he serves himself.”

Mr. Paxton’s campaign and office did not respond to that criticism or to questions about his travel, security or personal finances.

He has long denied any wrongdoing. Several of his trips were to conferences with other attorneys general. Mr. Paxton also has traveled frequently to Washington during a career in which he brought dozens of lawsuits against the Biden and Obama administrations.

Mr. Paxton’s allies say criticism of his travel unfairly distracts from his record battling for conservative causes.

“What does that have to do with his ability to take on the Obama administration and win cases?” said Bob Hall, a Republican state senator. “Ken Paxton has gotten the job done, and I think that’s what is important.”

Mr. Talarico has not reported accepting any gifts while in office. In a form filed with the U.S. Senate in August, he said he earned about $51,500 as a state lawmaker and about $33,000 from a consulting firm from January 2025 to May 2026. He also reported several mutual funds and a book deal for an unspecified amount. In a separate form filed in Texas, Mr. Talarico listed one piece of property.

Security costs for Mr. Paxton’s travel since 2015 have exceeded $3.1 million, according to state records, which do not specify whether a trip is related to his official duties. That tally does not include other travel-related expenses charged to taxpayers. He has visited nearly 225 cities, making multiple trips to destinations like Park City, Utah, and New Orleans. Security costs peaked in 2024 at more than $483,000.

Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, has also traveled across the country and abroad, with security costs topping $5.4 million since 2015, records show.

“Business or pleasure — security detail goes,” said Arnold Alejandro, a former member of the state security detail who protected Mr. Paxton and other Texas officials. “I don’t care if it’s the Bahamas on vacation in a bikini or Washington, D.C.”

A recent ProPublica investigation found records indicating a work-related purpose for only one in six of the locations logged by Mr. Paxton’s security team. Mr. Alejandro added that many politicians, including Mr. Paxton, mixed business and personal activities while away from the office.

“You schedule one meeting with a politician or state representative and then you go play — you have dinners, you have sightseeing, but as long as you call it state business, it’s business,” he said.

Chris Toth, who served as a top official of the National Association of Attorneys General for 18 years, called Mr. Paxton’s travel “incredibly excessive.”

“It’s beyond the pale of anything that’s ever been brought to my attention,” said Mr. Toth, an outspoken critic of Mr. Paxton. “When you are running an office the size of the Texas attorney general’s office, it’s very demanding, and there is a cost to being out of the office.”

Security for a 2017 trip by Mr. Paxton to Israel, which was organized by the national attorneys general group, cost nearly $75,000 and was one of his most expensive trips. Mr. Toth said Mr. Paxton insisted on his own security detail even though the Israeli government provided protection for the entire delegation, which included six other attorneys general. Mr. Paxton also traveled in a separate vehicle from the rest of the group, Mr. Toth said.

Records show the attorney general’s security team also accompanied him to Louisville, Ky., in May 2024, when Mr. Paxton was photographed at the Kentucky Derby with a group that included Tracy Duhon, an aspiring Christian influencer he is currently dating. Security for that trip cost $13,235. One month later, Mr. Paxton and his wife, Angela, separated, according to her divorce petition the following year, which accused him of adultery.

In response to questions from The Times about security costs for Mr. Paxton’s trips to Louisville, Israel and other destinations, the Department of Public Safety called the expenses “appropriate” and in line with the agency’s “strict standards.”

It’s unclear how often Mr. Paxton has traveled without Texas law enforcement, but a few foreign trips that were not listed in state logs drew media attention.

In 2019, he traveled to China with other attorneys general and met with government officials there, despite warnings from staffers about surveillance by the communist government, according to Fox News. In 2023, The Associated Press reported that Mr. Paxton went to Qatar for the World Cup.

Another foreign trip not reported in state security logs: Mr. Paxton’s excursion in 2024 to Dubai, where he celebrated New Year’s Eve with two fugitives wanted on federal fraud charges, according to a lawsuit and video from the party. Ms. Duhon also appears in the video and in photos with Mr. Paxton in Europe this past summer; she has declined interview requests. Mr. Paxton’s campaign did not respond to questions about who paid for the Dubai trip.

In a rare instance in which Mr. Paxton faced questions about his travel in a public forum, state senators grilled him in February 2021 about his appearance at the pro-Trump rally that preceded the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol. Mr. Paxton declined to say who paid for his trip to Washington. “I didn’t spend money personally,” said Mr. Paxton, who had tried to help President Trump overturn the 2020 election.

Mr. Paxton’s security detail spent about $7,000 to go to Washington in January 2021, though it’s not certain that trip included the rally since the logs do not specify exact dates.

Robert Nichols, one of two Republican state senators who voted to convict Mr. Paxton at his 2023 impeachment trial, said elected officials should expect rigorous scrutiny of their travel.

“Most people would ask who is paying for these trips,” he said. “Why is he gone all the time? It’s not like he’s selling economic development.”

Shortly after he took office as attorney general in 2015, Mr. Paxton was indicted on securities-fraud charges. Because the allegations were not connected to his job, he could not use tax dollars or campaign donations to pay for his lawyers. Instead, he accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars from about 50 people, including campaign donors, for a legal defense fund. He relied on an exemption in state law that allows government officials to take gifts from people with whom they have an existing relationship, separate from their public office.

In 2017, a $100,000 donation to the fund from an executive under investigation for health care fraud led to bribery allegations against Mr. Paxton. The prosecutor handling the case, Erleigh Wiley, ended the inquiry after Mr. Paxton’s attorneys argued that he had an existing relationship with the donor.

“If you’re going to take down a big fish, you better make sure you can go all the way,” Ms. Wiley said.

Mr. Paxton later cut a deal in which the securities-fraud charges were dropped and he did not admit guilt.

His impeachment trial, in which he was acquitted, centered on allegations that Mr. Paxton had misused the power of his office to help a donor in legal trouble who had paid for expensive renovations to Mr. Paxton’s home. In the lead-up to the trial, one of Mr. Paxton’s top aides said the attorney general had asked him to review the donor’s case — during a call from a Mexican resort town.

“He always cared about what trip he was going on, who was taking him to dinner,” the aide, Blake Brickman, told investigators for the Texas House. “He likes the perks of the office.”

Other high-level staffers also described what they said was Mr. Paxton’s penchant for freeloading during the investigation that led to his impeachment. David Maxwell, Mr. Paxton’s director of law enforcement, accused the attorney general of charging a $600 sport coat in a hotel gift shop to a conference organizer. “He always had his hand out,” Mr. Maxwell said.

As criticism of his lifestyle has mounted during the Senate campaign, Mr. Paxton has tried to remind voters of his humble upbringing as the son of an Air Force pilot.

“Growing up, we lived in a white trailer with no air conditioning outside of an Air Force base,” Mr. Paxton said at the Republican Party’s convention in Dallas last month. “We didn’t have much but I learned more about service to my country in that trailer than I did in any classroom.”

Now, his real estate holdings — the target of attacks by Mr. Talarico — include four condominiums at a luxury resort in Utah, three homes in Florida and a plot of land in Hawaii.

And photos on social media offer a glimpse of his cross-country travel, including a black-tie charity event in Palm Beach, Fla., and a luxury golf resort in South Carolina.

During Mr. Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, a men’s clothing store near Dallas, Lombardo Custom Apparel, posted a photo of Mr. Paxton in a tuxedo.

“We started doing his clothes a couple years ago as he started to build a pretty nice wardrobe,” said the owner, Jay Lombardo. “He’s trying to look the part as he runs for office.”

item.title: Last Ditch, a Bar Whose Mask Policy Tore It Apart, Will Close
item.description:
A Western Massachusetts bar at the center of a Covid masking controversy last month is moving toward closing down, according to a message it posted Monday on social media.

The bar, the Last Ditch, said on its website that it was founded for lesbians, as well as “transexuals, gender freaks, workers and their friends,” an oasis for safe and happy drinking in the tiny city of Greenfield. It became internationally known for the backlash to its owners’ decision to relax a mandatory face mask policy. The hope was that making masks optional on Saturdays would increase business. But opponents of the change argued the bar was abandoning its goals to be welcoming to everyone.

People posting online accused the owners of being ableist and risking the lives of immunocompromised customers. A backlash to the backlash quickly emerged, with people mocking customers and their Covid concerns.

A Boston Globe story in September on the masking dispute went viral, and the travails of the Last Ditch were published by media around the country and overseas.

The publicity appeared to draw dozens of potential customers to the first mask-optional Saturday night after the local controversy became widely known. But the burst of attention was apparently not enough to save the bar in downtown Greenfield, a city of about 17,000 people.

A message on the Last Ditch Instagram page said that the bar needed “new owners ASAP.”

“We are SOFT CLOSING effective immediately, all BOOKED events will CONTINUE, otherwise we are CLOSED,” the message read. “Love and solidarity to all.”

“We have put our lives on hold to foster networks of care, resources, and a home base for organizing,” the posting said. “It’s time we pass it on.”

The bar’s social media listed several scheduled events this week, including an open mic night and karaoke.

Three housemates, Asa Rosario, Jackie Matellian and Sage Territo, opened the bar in 2025, hoping to fill a need after two queer bars in the region had closed in recent years.

A message to the bar’s email account on Monday returned an automated response saying, “We are community run for the community, so we are slow to reply.”

Amy Cahillane, the community and economic development director for Greenfield, said Monday that “it is always a shame to lose a small business,” especially one that was a valuable part of the city’s downtown.

item.title: Teen Arrested in Florida Shooting Will Be Tried as Adult, Officials Say
item.description:
A 15-year-old boy who was arrested in the shooting of 11 people after a college football game in Tallahassee, Fla., will stand trial as an adult, a Florida prosecutor said on Monday.

The teenager, Anthony Rivers III, was ordered to remain in custody at a juvenile court hearing on Monday after his arrest the day before. The shooting took place in a crowded, closed-off street on Saturday about an hour after Florida A&M University’s homecoming game. A crowd of just over 20,000 attended the event.

The shooting left six people hospitalized as of Sunday, one of whom was in critical condition. A spokesman for the Leon County School District said four of its students were wounded, including the one in critical condition.

Six of the 11 people shot were minors, the Tallahassee Police Department said. A 12th person was injured but not shot, officials said.

Lawrence Revell, chief of the Tallahassee police, said at a news conference on Monday that the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a physical altercation between people who knew one another, and that none of the victims appeared to be intended targets. He said more arrests were possible.

Judge Andrew Sheeran, who presided over Monday’s hearing, said he would grant the request of the top prosecutor in Tallahassee to try Mr. Rivers as an adult, which Florida law allows in certain cases. He will be charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and one count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, officials said.

“It’s our discretion because of the severity of the offense,” said the prosecutor, Jack Campbell. In a phone interview, he added that he had discussed the decision with juvenile-case prosecutors before asking his prosecutors to review the case. “Ultimately, it was my decision.”

Mr. Rivers, dressed in a white T-shirt, gray gym shorts, sandals and his hair pulled up into a bun, stood quietly at Monday’s hearing with his hands clasped behind his back, as the public defender who is representing him addressed the court.

The public defender said she had previously represented Mr. Rivers. Her office did not reply to a request for comment. Efforts to reach relatives of Mr. Rivers were not immediately successful.

According to court records, Mr. Rivers has been arrested previously on charges including burglary and theft of a gun, but it was unclear what the outcome was. He was arrested on Sept. 6 for violating his probation and had been sentenced to a juvenile home.

According to a police affidavit, Mr. Rivers was arrested after surveillance cameras and an ankle monitor he was wearing identified him at a Tallahassee mall where gunfire had erupted in an underground parking lot.

The police identified another 15-year-old who was with Mr. Rivers as the shooter, according to the affidavit. Nobody was injured in the shooting, which occurred after an altercation in the mall.

Mr. Campbell declined to discuss anything about Mr. Rivers’s criminal record. But he said if someone was a repeat offender, “that’s something we consider” when determining whether to charge a juvenile as an adult.

The shooting echoed others in Tallahassee in recent years. Nine people were shot — one fatally — outside a liquor store in 2022 that Mr. Campbell said was connected to a homecoming event at Florida A&M.

Last year, two people were killed and six others were wounded in a shooting at Florida State University, which is adjacent to Florida A&M. Mr. Campbell is seeking the death penalty against the shooter in that case, Phoenix Ikner, who has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.

The shooting on Saturday could have been much worse, Mr. Campbell said. It happened on Perry Street, a residential street that runs alongside Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the football team plays. The street was blocked off for vendors selling food and T-shirts, and it is a popular place to tailgate before and after games.

“If you go to FAMU, you’ve spent time on Perry Street,” Mr. Campbell said.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Election Day Is Next Week. What Can Early Voting Tell Us So Far?
item.description:
Tens of millions of Americans have already cast their ballots in the 2026 elections, and while polling has pointed to a good night for Democrats, there are plenty of pressing questions that won’t be answered until election night, or beyond.

It can be tempting to turn to the early vote for answers to these questions. But in most cases, early voting data is limited in how much insight it can offer. The data tells us which voters have turned out, not for whom they have been persuaded to vote — to say nothing of how voters’ behaviors have shifted since the last election cycle. And it offers no insight into what turnout will be like on Election Day.

Nonetheless, there are some early voting takeaways worth monitoring.

Around 80 percent of Texans cast their ballots ahead of Election Day in 2024, making the early vote a more useful assessment of the political environment there than in many other states. And Texas has drawn a great deal of attention in these midterms, with polls in the state’s Senate race showing James Talarico, the Democrat, tied with or narrowly leading Ken Paxton.

Voters in Texas do not register with a political party, but the state does record voters’ participation in a partisan primary. By that metric, Democrats are faring well in the advance vote: In votes cast through Saturday, Democratic primary voters outnumbered Republican primary voters by around two percentage points, based on New York Times estimates.

But that wouldn’t be entirely unexpected. More voters cast ballots in the state’s Democratic primary in March than did so in the concurrent Republican primary, a striking feat. Among the largest caveats with early voting data, though, is that participation in a party’s primary is no guarantee of a vote for that party in a general election — and around one in four voters have no history of primary participation.

More than four million ballots have been cast in Texas thus far, a strong turnout showing that more closely resembles a presidential election than a midterm. Turnout in the state’s Hispanic areas has been particularly high — through the end of Saturday, majority-Hispanic counties were running at around 90 percent of their 2024 pace, compared to 82 percent statewide. (Midterms often see a much starker decrease in turnout.)

While few swing states have seen numbers as robust as Texas, turnout is generally higher across the board than it was in the 2022 midterms, with the largest increases in less populous states that are more competitive than usual this cycle, like Iowa, Kansas and Maine. (Maine, like Texas, is running at around 80 percent of its 2024 pace.)

The increase is particularly notable in Kansas, which had highly competitive races for governor and attorney general in 2022. With a competitive Senate race this year, turnout is up by around 50 percent, and registered Democrats make up a greater share of the electorate than at this point in 2022 or 2024. The results may not necessarily be representative: Johnson County, which leans Democratic and is the most populous county in the state, typically constitutes around 25 percent of the statewide vote, but makes up nearly half of the advance votes thus far.

Georgia and North Carolina, where polls have shown Democratic Senate candidates with wider advantages, are among a handful of states that include race in their voter files, and a large majority of ballots in each are cast before Election Day. That makes them particularly useful for examining how Black voters are turning out relative to past cycles.

The racial composition of the electorate doesn’t neatly correlate with election results, but even a small increase in Black vote share would be a strong sign for Democrats — Times Voter Trends estimates that Kamala Harris won around 90 percent of Black voters in Georgia and North Carolina in 2024.

In both states, the share of Black voters casting their ballots ahead of Election Day has paced ahead of 2022 and 2024 totals, and has largely remained consistent throughout the early voting period.

item.title: Manhunt Begins After Convicted Murderer Escapes From Tennessee Prison
item.description:
A manhunt was underway on Monday for an inmate who had escaped from a correctional facility in Tennessee, where he was serving a life sentence for murder, officials said.

The man, Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was discovered to be missing around 11:30 p.m. on Sunday at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tenn., about 125 miles north of Memphis, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement Monday morning.

The New York Times

Staff members immediately searched the prison, the statement said. A review of the security cameras showed Mr. Morley had breached the complex’s perimeter fence and fled in his prison uniform, officials said.

The department said it was working with local, state and federal law enforcement officials to find Mr. Morley. Buildings and structures near the prison have been searched and cleared, officials said. The Tennessee Highway Patrol deployed aerial support and state troopers to assist with the search, the department said.

Mr. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder in 2025 in the death of Cody Birchfield, who had been reported missing in February 2022, according to the TV news station WJHL in Johnson City, Tenn.

Mr. Morley was arrested in North Carolina in March 2022. WJHL reported that after he was taken into custody, deputies searched Mr. Morley’s home and found Mr. Birchfield’s body there.

Prison records show Mr. Morley had also been convicted of aggravated burglary and tampering with evidence. Records also show that Mr. Morley was convicted of evading arrest in 2022 and of vandalism in 2024.

He was added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation’s Most Wanted list after his escape, the corrections department said. Officials are offering a reward of up to $2,500 for information leading to Mr. Morley’s arrest.

item.title: Justice Dept. Brings More Charges Against Comey, Accusing Him of Leaks
item.description:
Federal prosecutors have brought new charges against James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director, accusing him of mishandling national security information in October 2016 that they said ended up in a New York Times article, according to court papers unsealed on Monday.

The case highlights the extraordinary effort the Justice Department has expended in pursuing Mr. Comey, a vocal critic of President Trump’s who has emerged as one of his most favored targets. It is the third time in 13 months that the Trump administration has sought to prosecute Mr. Comey, whom Mr. Trump fired as F.B.I. director in 2017.

The new charges came in the form of a criminal information filed under seal in Federal District Court in Washington this month, the court records say, meaning that prosecutors brought charges without immediately seeking approval from either a judge or a grand jury. Mr. Comey’s lawyers had in recent weeks sought to get the charges dismissed, but have yet to succeed, the records show.

In a video posted online, Mr. Comey vowed to fight the case.

“I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people,” he said. The new case against him, he said, “would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”

The charging document was signed by two senior officials at Justice Department headquarters, as well as lower-ranking line prosecutors on special assignments from other offices, including the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. attorney offices in Texas and Florida.

Mr. Comey is accused of knowingly and willfully causing national defense information to be “communicated, delivered and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it” around Oct. 4 and 5 of 2016. Court papers in the case point to an Oct. 5 article in The Times describing a novel use of surveillance authority involving Yahoo emails.

Lawyers for Mr. Comey said in court papers that the issue had twice been investigated, including during the first Trump administration, and had not led to charges either time.

The article described how Yahoo used a system intended to scan emails for child pornography and spam to help satisfy a secret court order requiring it to search for messages containing a computer “signature” tied to the communications of a state-sponsored terrorist organization, citing several people familiar with the matter.

According to the article, the Justice Department obtained an individualized order from a judge of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, and Yahoo was barred from disclosing the matter.

Prosecutors, in court papers, said that the Times article came about because Mr. Comey “sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before.” The investigation, the prosecutors said, “uncovered evidence that Mr. Comey directed staff to speak to” The Times “about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”

Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesman for The Times, said the paper “does not comment on the sourcing behind our reporting, but we know from experience that prosecutions like this one are designed to discourage sources from providing journalists with the kind of valuable and illuminating information that the public needs to know.”

Mr. Comey’s legal team is fighting the case partly on the grounds that the administration already bungled it by not filing an indictment before the 10-year statute of limitations. His lawyers say that time limit applies to indictments, not a charging instrument like a criminal information, which typically would precede an indictment by a grand jury or a guilty plea.

Trump administration officials have faced resistance from grand jurors in the nation’s capital, who have repeatedly rejected some cases that seemed to be motivated by presidential animus.

Because prosecutors have yet to secure an indictment, and it has been more than 10 years since the events in question, the charges should be dismissed, Mr. Comey’s lawyers say.

The charges add to the number of actions the Justice Department has taken on politically sensitive matters in the days before midterm elections. Typically, the department has sought to stay quiet in the two months preceding an election, to avoid the appearance of trying to influence voters.

In the past month alone, the Justice Department has searched the home of Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat; secured an indictment against a powerful Virginia state legislator and members of her family; and brought charges against two former F.B.I. officials accused of falsely minimizing their work on investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of the former president.

The Justice Department has had a spotty record to date in its pursuit of Mr. Comey. It secured an indictment against him in September 2025, accusing him of lying over years-old testimony to Congress. The charges were later thrown out by a judge.

A second case in North Carolina is set to go to trial next year, after prosecutors in Virginia rejected it. That case centers on a photograph of seashells on a beach that Mr. Comey shared to social media last year. The shells were arranged to say “86 47,” which prosecutors deemed a threat against Mr. Trump.

In an unusual twist, the new charges were unsealed hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Trump administration had unlawfully fired Mr. Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, from her job as a prosecutor in that city. The administration, the judge found, had acted in violation of the Constitution and federal law when it claimed that the president had wide latitude to fire civil servants.

item.title: The Other Dan Sullivan Fires Back at Trump’s Lawsuit in Alaska
item.description:
The other Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s Senate race, who has said relatively little despite being at the center of a legal and political maelstrom, defended his position on the ballot in rare public comments on Monday.

The long-shot candidacy of Mr. Sullivan, a retired elementary schoolteacher who lives in a small Alaskan fishing village called Petersburg, has attracted outsize national attention because he has the same name as the state’s incumbent Republican senator. Republicans have accused Mr. Sullivan of Petersburg of being a spoiler aimed at confusing voters to help Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee. He was briefly removed from the ballot until a state court reinstated him.

The Justice Department, on President Trump’s order, filed a lawsuit last week seeking to block the certification of the race if votes for the former schoolteacher prevent the incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, from winning. Election law specialists have been skeptical of the litigation’s merits.

On Monday, the lesser-known Mr. Sullivan told a reporter for The Alaska Beacon that the lawsuit was “a gross misuse of the Justice Department for a situation that has already been litigated and resolved by the Alaska Supreme Court.”

“I think the Division of Elections did a notable job of differentiating two candidates on the ballot with similar names and the primary showed there was little if any confusion,” Mr. Sullivan wrote to the reporter, who interviewed him over email on behalf of a wider group of interested news outlets. “Alaskan voters are smart and I have faith in their ability to make an informed decision on their ballots.”

Throughout it all, Mr. Sullivan, the former teacher, has maintained that he is not part of a Democratic plot. He has not campaigned and has done few interviews.

His motivations have been the subject of intense scrutiny. He told The New York Times in August that he had previously voted for Democratic candidates for president and for Ms. Peltola during her previous runs for statewide office. Although he registered with the Republican Party at the same time as announcing his Senate run, he said he was a moderate Republican running in good faith, unhappy with the senator’s tenure and with Mr. Trump.

On Monday, the state elections division confirmed that Mr. Sullivan had changed his party registration from Republican to “undeclared” when filling out an absentee ballot form in the primary.

He at first told the Alaska Beacon reporter that he had not changed his registration. But when the switch was describd to him, he replied via email, “holy cow.. I did! - I can only guess I was thinking that since they didn’t affiliate me on the ballot, i should go with that but to be honest with you, I am frazzled by all of this.”

He said that he was a bit overwhelmed by all of the attention, and planned to have a quiet election night with a handful of close supporters and friends.

“To say that it has now become overwhelming and intimidating is an understatement,” Mr. Sullivan wrote. “It is unending stress, at times paralyzing and I am looking forward to it being over.”

A spokesman for the incumbent Mr. Sullivan said after the lawsuit was filed that “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska.”

item.title: Trump Dangles $1 Million Reward for Reporting Voter Fraud
item.description:
As President Trump has implored voters to support Republicans in next week’s elections, he has frequently dangled financial incentives and issued unfounded warnings about voter fraud.

On Monday, he married those two passions.

“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” Mr. Trump wrote on social media.

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about where the money would come from for the ostensible rewards or how Americans are supposed to report fraud accusations.

The announcement reflected another step in Mr. Trump’s gathering campaign to use the powers of his office to influence the outcome of the midterms.

For years, the president has attacked the integrity of U.S. elections, and in his second term, his administration has tried to assert more control over the voting process, which is overseen by states. Last week, Mr. Trump moved to pre-emptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate loses.

The president and his Justice Department have also leaned on expansive but unsupported claims of voter fraud in trying to force states like California to set aside thousands of mail ballots they claim were sent to noncitizens.

At the same time, Mr. Trump has stepped up the financial incentives for voters as Republicans face increasingly steep odds of keeping control of Congress.

A national poll from The New York Times and Siena University found Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit a new low this month, with just 36 percent of likely voters saying they approved of his job performance. Likely voters said they preferred Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points in their congressional districts.

Over the past two months, Mr. Trump has signed pardons at campaign rallies, sent $500 Obamacare “refund” checks” and issued $90 direct deposits to seniors to offset Medicare premiums.

The central reward, though, is the so-called “Trump Dividend,” which Mr. Trump announced at the Republican gathering he insisted his party throw last month in Dallas.

Mr. Trump has promised $5,000 for every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, a proposal that has drawn bipartisan criticism and would cost more than $1 trillion. It would also likely require congressional approval.

Earlier this month, Mr. Trump announced a new $25 million whistle-blower incentive program to provide information to combat fraud. There are already multiple avenues for reporting fraud to the federal government, and the new program raised concerns because Mr. Trump said he would personally determine who received the money.

item.title: Ohio State Professor Who Shoved a Filmmaker on Campus Resigns
item.description:
The Ohio State University professor who was accused in February of shoving a documentary filmmaker to the ground resigned last week, the university confirmed on Monday.

The professor, Luke M. Perez, who taught at an Ohio State center designed to promote civic engagement and intellectual diversity, was accused of attacking the filmmaker, Michael Newman, after Mr. Newman tried to ask additional questions to E. Gordon Gee, a former Ohio State president who was being interviewed.

As the interview in a campus building was ending, Mr. Newman asked to pose “one more question” to Dr. Gee.

At that point, according to court papers, Dr. Perez slapped Mr. Newman’s phone out of his hand, struck his face and shoved him into a wall.

Dr. Perez had initially been charged with assault, but pleaded no contest in July to a reduced charge of disorderly conduct. His resignation was reported earlier by The Columbus Dispatch.

Jeffrey Vardaro, who is representing Mr. Newman in a related lawsuit, called Dr. Perez’s resignation a “positive development.” But he added that he believed Ohio State should take responsibility for the episode.

“It’s a really dark message that they’re sending to the public and the students when the First Amendment or free speech center, or however it’s portrayed, is not itself open to free speech,” Mr. Vardaro said.

Ohio State declined to comment beyond confirming the resignation.

The Salmon P. Chase Center, where Dr. Perez was a professor, was formed by the Ohio Legislature in 2023 with the stated purpose of “encouraging academic freedom and free speech.”

In his ongoing federal case against Dr. Perez and Christopher Green, an Ohio State law professor, Mr. Newman also accused Mr. Green of making false statements to the police suggesting that he was the aggressor in the February incident. Lawyers for Dr. Perez and Mr. Green did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Based on Mr. Green’s false statements, according to the lawsuit, the police at first focused their investigation on Mr. Newman. They elected to bring charges against Dr. Perez after interviewing Mr. Newman and viewing the video footage, the lawsuit said.

The incident was filmed by a local journalist, D.J. Byrnes, who is behind a left-leaning website called The Rooster that often skewers local politicians.

Mr. Byrnes was himself the target of a recent criminal case that also tested the limits of free speech, after he sent a message containing a lewd image of Shrek to a state senator.

Mr. Newman had been working on a documentary focusing on controversies at Ohio State, including allegations involving connections between the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and one of the university’s major donors, the businessman Leslie Wexner.

Mr. Wexner has repeatedly denied knowledge or involvement in any of Mr. Epstein’s criminal activities.

item.title: Appeals Court Declines to Intervene in California Ballot Lawsuit
item.description:
A federal appeals court on Monday rejected a request from the Trump administration that it intervene in a lawsuit against California and declined to immediately order the state to set aside as many as 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claimed had been provided to noncitizens.

By a 2-1 vote, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found that it was too early for the appeals court to take up the case because a lower court judge had not yet considered it, refusing the Trump administration’s effort to rush the case by leapfrogging a district court judge.

The ruling came as the federal government waged an increasingly coercive pressure campaign against California, attempting to enlist the state in its hunt for instances of voter fraud and sowing doubt about the security of its voter registration processes.

In the order on Monday, which did not address the underlying merits of the Trump administration’s claims, Judge Mark J. Bennett, who was appointed by President Trump, joined with Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, who was appointed by Joseph R. Biden Jr. They wrote that the Justice Department “failed to allow” a lower court the “adequate opportunity” to consider the case, rushing an appeal before a district court judge could hold a hearing, which is scheduled for Tuesday.

While the ruling was only an incremental setback for the Trump administration, the appeals court had already flashed skepticism about the lawsuit during an emergency hearing on Sunday — suggesting skepticism about the ultimate success of the administration’s gambit in California.

Both Judge Bennett and Judge Sanchez lobbed tough questions at a government lawyer about the justifications for asking California to screen ballots and the extreme urgency it had claimed in the lawsuit. In the order, they noted that an eleventh hour ruling — days before the midterm election — would also “undoubtedly” interfere with the state’s ability to administer the election, potentially violating a doctrine repeatedly upheld by the Supreme Court that federal courts should not change rules on the eve of the vote.

Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, a second Trump appointee on the panel, wrote that he would have granted the Trump administration’s request, and that its claims that thousands of noncitizens may be voting in the election should be taken seriously.

“The question — does the federal government have the power to stop this potential attack on the integrity of our elections?” he wrote. “Under both federal law and the Constitution, the answer must be ‘yes.’”

California officials welcomed the ruling, even as the lawsuit was set to continue almost immediately in federal district court.

“The court’s order serves as an important step in our efforts to protect Californians’ right to vote and our state’s authority to run fair and secure elections,” Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, said in a statement. “All the evidence — counts, recounts, hand counts, audits — shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare.”

Monday’s order emphasized that the Trump administration had lodged its appeal even though there were still days to spare before the deadline the government had initially set in requesting court action. When it filed the lawsuit against California, the Justice Department asked the lower court to reach a preliminary decision in the case by Election Day, Nov. 3.

In court filings, the Justice Department indicated that it had come up with the list of about 20,000 names by comparing some California voter roll data with a federal immigration database, matching names and checking for overlaps that would indicate that people listed at one point as noncitizens in federal data had also appeared as registered voters.

California officials have complained that the administration has been vague about its exact process for coming up with the names and the list includes errors. It is already illegal under state and federal law for noncitizens to vote in federal elections in California. Voters are required to attest they are citizens when registering.

The administration’s claims have also been a moving target.

In July, officials had claimed to have found as many as 270,000 noncitizens on voter rolls in Nevada, California, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

In a letter that month, it warned California officials it had found “as many as 190,832 noncitizens registered to vote.” When California officials challenged the finding and asked for more information, the Trump administration did not respond, the state said in a filing.

On Oct. 13, the Justice Department delivered a smaller list containing 20,000 names to officials in Los Angeles County. Officials there noted that the list contained addresses of people throughout the state, and only 7,035 records appeared to be from Los Angeles.

Two days after it sent the voter file to Los Angeles, the Justice Department filed suit to stop the counting of ballots sent to the 20,000 individuals it flagged “until their citizenship status can be determined.”

In a filing to the appeals court, the state said the data it received would need to be manually reviewed to make sure that lawful voters were not disenfranchised. The effort, it wrote, would “redirect key staff from the critical work of administering the Nov. 3 election.”

Election officials said they also launched a hurried effort to review the data within the 48 hours the Justice Department gave officials to act. In court filings, they reported that cursory review of about 3 percent of the records showed the federal data appeared to be riddled with incorrect leads. Fewer than half, they said were active voters. Most had never voted at all. Importantly, more than 25 percent listed a birthplace in the United States, making them definitively citizens.

When officials in Nevada interrogated similar claims from the administration, it similarly found problems with the data. The Trump administration said in July that nearly 16,000 noncitizens were registered to vote in the state, it followed up with a list of 185 voters it said it “confirmed” were illegally registered. The state later determined that all were lawful citizens.

Laurel Rosenhall contributed reporting.

item.title: Bob Woodward Thought Jeff Bezos Had His Back. Now He Feels Disillusioned.
item.description:
When Bob Woodward, the veteran star Washington Post reporter of Watergate fame, was about to publish a hard-hitting book about President Trump in 2018, he called the owner of his newspaper, Jeff Bezos, to warn him.

“Don’t worry, I have your back, Bob,” Mr. Bezos told him. “I’ll always have your back.”

“Always” turned out not to be as long as it used to be, Mr. Woodward now says he discovered. After more than a half-century breaking stories about Washington, one of the scoops in Mr. Woodward’s new memoir is his own breakup in all but name with Mr. Bezos, who in his view turned out to not have the backs of the journalists working for him, after all.

Instead, Mr. Woodward writes, Mr. Bezos has been “compromising public trust in The Washington Post’s aggressive and independent journalism” in deference to Mr. Trump. While he says Mr. Bezos has not interfered in news stories, Mr. Woodward writes that the billionaire owner’s sweeping staff cuts, reorientation of the editorial page and personal ingratiation to the president have betrayed the legacy of a newspaper known for courageous coverage.

The condemnation of Mr. Bezos by his most famous employee is one of the headlines from “Secrets,” the long-awaited memoir of his 55 years in journalism to be published Nov. 24 by Mr. Woodward, who still holds the title of associate editor at the paper.

A copy of the memoir was obtained by The New York Times. Here are six takeaways:

For decades, Mr. Woodward guarded the identity of the sources of his blockbuster stories and best selling books. But now, he finally names names. Many of his early sources have died, and he received permission from others still alive to identify them.

While W. Mark Felt, the former deputy F.B.I. director, unmasked himself in 2005 as the famous Watergate source called Deep Throat, much of Washington will pore through this new book to learn who else talked. It turns out that lots of people did, including presidents, cabinet secretaries, generals, spymasters, Supreme Court justices and F.B.I. agents.

Mr. Woodward discloses for the first time his sources for one of the most iconic scenes he ever reported, a moment shortly before Richard M. Nixon resigned because of Watergate, when the sobbing president asked Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger to fall to his knees and pray with him.

The sources, the book now reveals, were two of Mr. Kissinger’s lieutenants, Brent Scowcroft and Lawrence S. Eagleburger. While neither was present for the scene, Mr. Kissinger described it to them shortly afterward and the two then listened in on the phone when Mr. Nixon called Mr. Kissinger to ask him not to tell anyone he had cried.

Mr. Woodward also describes lengthy conversations with two of Mr. Nixon’s own lawyers, J. Fred Buzhardt Jr. and Leonard Garment, neither of whom seemed to hold their client in high regard. “He flat out lies,” Mr. Buzhardt told Mr. Woodward. Mr. Garment separately told Mr. Woodward that Mr. Nixon was “a very strange man, very strange” and “guilty of misdemeanors.” By not destroying his secret Oval Office tapes, Mr. Nixon was “letting America into the toilet of his mind,” Mr. Garment said. “The impeachable offense was letting us all see.”

The new memoir also describes Mr. Woodward’s closeness with Richard G. Darman, a key Republican official under multiple presidents who became both one of his best sources and best friends. As excerpted in The New Yorker, the conflict ultimately led to a rupture after Mr. Woodward published a harsh series on President George H.W. Bush’s economic policies shortly before the 1992 election, based in part on Mr. Darman’s descriptions.

One of Mr. Woodward’s earliest books was “The Brethren,” a penetrating look inside the normally secretive chambers of the Supreme Court, written with Scott Armstrong, that stunned the legal world and beyond. For years, lawyers and judges wondered how Mr. Woodward got inside one of the most tightly guarded institutions in Washington.

In “Secrets,” Mr. Woodward discloses the names of five justices who spoke with the authors, all of whom have since died: Potter Stewart, Lewis F. Powell Jr., Byron R. White, Harry A. Blackmun and William H. Rehnquist. And he describes how he obtained one of the documents that informed the book: a secret history of the Nixon Watergate tapes case, which revealed the internal debate among the justices over how to rule.

He went to the home of Steven P. Goldberg, who was a clerk to Justice William J. Brennan Jr. and had authored the case history, but refused to give it to Mr. Woodward. The reporter convinced him to instead read it to him, which Mr. Goldberg proceeded to do. But it was long and Mr. Woodward took his time scribbling down notes. Finally, an exhausted Mr. Goldberg nodded off.

Mr. Woodward waited 20 minutes so that Mr. Goldberg would reach a deep sleep. He decided not to simply take the document — “that seemed a little too far, even for me” — so he nudged Mr. Goldberg and simply told him that he would borrow it and bring it back the next morning. The groggy clerk stirred and mumbled his assent. Mr. Woodward wrote that he did his best not to race out the door with the document. “If I was on a security camera I wanted to be behaving properly, with whatever might be left of my dignity,” he writes.

Mr. Woodward also writes about encounters with more recent justices. He reports that his wife, Elsa Walsh, a former journalist for The Post and The New Yorker, sat next to former Justice Stephen G. Breyer at a dinner and he told her that he was “forced out” to make way for someone younger on the court.

He also recalls running into Justice Elena Kagan at a Washington party in 2023. Justice Kagan expressed admiration for “The Brethren” and Mr. Woodward noted that the main point was how the ideological center of the court in that era dominated. “Yes, I prefer it that way,” Justice Kagan said. “That’s exactly what it should be.”

When he asked her if she was happy on the court, Justice Kagan said no, she was not, given the situation.

For all his fame, Mr. Woodward is known in Washington as something of a closed door himself. He loves talking about reporting and politics, but has generally been reticent about his personal life. While this book, his 24th, is not exactly an exercise in introspection, at age 83 he finally opens up at least a bit more than he has done in public.

He recounts growing up in a broken home in Wheaton, Ill. He caught his mother kissing another man and then discovered that his parents were getting divorced when he rummaged through his father’s sock drawer and found a private letter. He writes that he “learned at a very young age the pain of secrets and how they can destroy lives and started down a path of trying to find them.”

Mr. Woodward also writes that a fire gutted his home as a child, leaving him so anxious to this day that he keeps multiple fire extinguishers throughout his Washington home. He describes finding a way as a young Navy officer to get out of a deployment to Vietnam, only to learn later that the man who went instead ended up dying. And he recalls falling out with his Watergate partner Carl Bernstein during the writing of their second book, “The Final Days,” and how it took years to repair the friendship.

Mr. Woodward addresses some of the controversies of his career. He insists that, despite denials and doubts, he did get into a hospital room to see a dying William J. Casey, the C.I.A. director in the 1980s — he was let in, he writes, by a security agent he had befriended. He publishes images of the notes that he took quoting Mr. Casey acknowledging a role in the Iran-contra affair by saying, “I believed.”

By contrast, he accepts blame for “my spectacular failure” as an editor in publishing a fabricated story by the Post reporter Janet Cooke about what turned out to be a fictional 8-year-old heroin addict. That incident convinced him “that I was not cut out to be an editor.”

One of the other mistakes in judgment Mr. Woodward acknowledges was his faith in Mr. Bezos. “I remember feeling relief when Jeff decided to buy The Post in 2013,” he writes. “I believed at the time that Bezos would provide the finances for The Post to continue to operate courageously.”

But his views began to change in 2024, when Mr. Bezos decided just before the election to pull an endorsement of Kamala Harris and declare that The Post would no longer endorse presidential candidates. “At the time, I thought, is he not reading his own newspaper or my books about Trump?” Mr. Woodward writes. The timing made it look “like Bezos and the newspaper were capitulating to Trump.”

Mr. Bezos then shifted the opinion pages to only advocate “personal liberties and free markets” with no dissenting views. “I could only imagine the agony this kind of decision would have caused Kay or Ben,” he adds, referring to Katharine Graham and Benjamin C. Bradlee, the publisher and executive editor during Watergate.

He came to believe that the “benefit of the doubt” that he had given Mr. Bezos was unwarranted. While he notes that The Post continues to produce aggressive coverage of Mr. Trump, Mr. Woodward laments that Mr. Bezos has not publicly defended independent journalism against the president’s campaign of intimidation the way that A.G. Sulzberger, publisher of The Times, has. “It pains me that Jeff Bezos has remained silent,” he writes. “It is not too late for media owners to prioritize moral courage over financial gain.”

A representative of Mr. Bezos did not respond to a request for comment. Matt Murray, The Post’s executive editor, said that he appreciated Mr. Woodward’s praise for the paper’s recent coverage and added that Mr. Bezos had never interfered in news reporting.

“With Jeff’s backing, the company is getting back in shape and poised for our best decade,” he said in a statement. “More than that, the Woodwards and Bernsteins of today are breaking consequential stories that have people talking about us in a way they haven’t in years, with total independence and encouragement from our owner.”

item.title: El-Sayed Campaign Distances Itself From Group’s Ad Critical of Israel
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, sought to distance himself on Monday from an outside group’s political ad that endorses him and attacks his Republican opponent over support of Israel, a longtime U.S. ally.

In the video ad, set in a grocery store, a woman tells a man, presumably her romantic partner, that he needs to return a carton of eggs to the shelf. The man then asks whether their kids “don’t like eggs anymore.”

“No, they like eggs,” the woman says. “But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.”

The man and woman then bemoan the cost to taxpayers of U.S. military aid to Israel, which amounted to more than $21 billion between fall 2023 and fall 2025, according to Brown University’s Costs of War Project.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign emphasized that the ad, created by a left-wing political action committee called Rebellion PAC, was “not affiliated in any way” with him or his candidacy.

“Abdul is focused on pushing back against Trump’s agenda that is raising prices for Michiganders,” the campaign said in a statement on Monday. “No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign.”

Dr. El-Sayed has been an outspoken critic of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, which was set off by the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed 1,200 people. The war has killed at least 74,000 people, according to Gaza health officials.

The ad, a version of which first ran in 2024, has garnered more than six million views since it was posted on X on Friday. On Monday, Representative Haley Stevens, a pro-Israel Democrat whom Dr. El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the Senate primary, publicly criticized it for what she called “fearmongering about Israel.”

The dust-up over the video highlighted the challenge that intraparty tensions over Israel have created for Dr. El-Sayed, who is seeking to win a seat in one of the country’s most competitive and pivotal Senate races. A progressive, Dr. El-Sayed has repeatedly criticized the pro-Israel Democratic establishment that Ms. Stevens represents and said he does not support U.S. military aid for Israel. In recent months, he has worked to win the support of Jewish voters, and hundreds signed a public-facing letter backing him.

While the ad has captured attention on social media, it does not have major spending behind it. Rebellion PAC has reported that it has spent just $4,000 on social media and digital advertising against Mr. Rogers, and it has not reported any spending to air the ad on television.

In the ad, a narrator attacks former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, who has said he will support Israel “unconditionally.”

The ad concludes by continuing its attack on Mr. Rogers, playing on commonplace Republican attack spots tying Democrats to nonbinary and transgender people.

“Mike Rogers is for they/them,” the narrator says as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and two of his far-right political allies, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, are displayed on the screen. “Abdul El-Sayed is for you.”

On Monday, Ms. Stevens said she disagreed with the way the ad tied Americans’ economic woes to the country’s spending on aid for Israel.

“Do we need to lower costs by building more homes, securing people’s health care, and creating a fairer federal tax code? Yes, we do!!” Ms. Stevens said in a post on X on Monday. “How we do so is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world.”

In a statement, a spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers, Abby Ronson, said that he was “for every single Michigander” and accused Dr. El-Sayed’s allies of spreading “anti-Israel hate.” A group of rabbis and Jewish voters who have criticized Dr. El-Sayed for his tone and stance on Israel, Nonnegotiable Michigan, argued the ad invoked “antisemitic tropes.”

Ms. Stevens, who has long been a vocal supporter of aid for Israel, benefited from more than $30 million in advertising spending by the super PAC arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the country’s most influential pro-Israel group, during the Senate primary. The same PAC has also spent significantly to bolster Mr. Rogers’s campaign in the general election.

Ms. Stevens’s response to the ad represented her clearest criticism yet of Dr. El-Sayed’s supporters since the acrimonious Senate primary. She has expressed reservations about his campaign in recent weeks, including when she sidestepped a question on CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday morning about whether she supports Dr. El-Sayed’s candidacy.

The ad was posted on X by Cenk Uygur, the host and chief executive of The Young Turks, a left-wing online news network. He originally registered Rebellion PAC to support a congressional run in 2020, according to Federal Election Commission filings. It first ran in 2024, as part of Mr. Uygur’s failed presidential campaign.

In an email to The New York Times, Mr. Uygur called criticism of the ad, including charges of antisemitism, “preposterous.”

“The ad never mentions Jewish people because it’s about the foreign government of Israel,” he wrote.

item.title: Judge Temporarily Blocks Further Alterations at D.C.’s East Potomac Park
item.description:
A federal judge temporarily barred the Interior Department on Monday from carrying out a variety of major alterations at East Potomac Park, finding that the government had been taking steps to initiate President Trump’s vision for a championship-level golf course on the property while passing off the work in court as routine maintenance.

The ruling followed a confrontation between the Justice Department and Judge Ana C. Reyes, who throughout October called several Trump administration officials and government lawyers to account for what she described as misrepresentations about the plan.

The clash underscored what had been one of the president’s less visible plans for transforming the capital, compared to his efforts to seize control of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and add a gilded ballroom to the White House. This, instead, was the overhaul of a municipal golf course and public park.

It culminated in a searing 70-page opinion issued on Monday, in which Judge Reyes wrote that much of what she had been told in court stood at odds with Mr. Trump’s public pronouncements about the golf course, which came even as officials were insisting that no long-term plan was settled.

“Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president,” she wrote. “Not to believe him that a cabinet secretary has ‘developed’ a federal land project. Not to believe him that the secretary’s agency will destroy a historic golf course already on the land.”

“And yet, here we are,” she added.

Mr. Trump railed against the ruling on social media late Monday, saying the course would be closed as scheduled. He vowed to “immediately appeal” the decision.

“The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project,” he wrote. “We are asking the D.C. Circuit Court for immediate remedy.”

Judge Reyes marveled that a local dispute over a golf course had spiraled into a broader examination of the Trump administration’s tactics, requiring judges to anticipate when and where the federal government might abruptly move to carry out the president’s personal goals and projects.

“It now forces the court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys,” she wrote. “This morass of different accounts concerns the future of the East Potomac Golf Course, a historic landmark.”

A group that included two Washington residents and a preservation society that sued to block an overhaul of the existing site had asked the court to prevent the administration from cutting down more trees after 400 were felled in one morning earlier this month.

Judge Reyes granted the request and went further, barring other actions that could indirectly destroy trees, including staging heavy machinery. She went to great lengths to impart her instructions in detail, an apparent attempt to prevent the administration from citing confusion or ambiguity to act without her involvement.

She required the government to notify the court at least 10 days before closing the course or making any “irreversible modification to any forms or features” to East Potomac Park, where the current course is, including changes to “the park’s landforms, vegetation, course design, hydrology, pathways, and structures.”

“This is a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm,” said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the group behind the lawsuit.

The dramatic changes that Mr. Trump has made to Washington loomed over the lawsuit from the beginning.

Throughout early interactions with Justice Department attorneys on the case, Judge Reyes stressed that she wanted to avoid surprises, after the president acted without warning last year to demolish the East Wing of the White House before courts could review the legality of the project.

At the same time, she said the lawsuit placed her in a difficult spot, because she did not view it as the role of federal courts to police minor decisions about management of federal lands. While Mr. Trump had mused since last year about transforming plans for East Potomac Park. But earlier this year Judge Reyes repeatedly told the group behind the lawsuit that it was not yet clear that the federal government was implementing his vision, making court action premature.

Hesitant to issue any order that would prevent rank-and-file government workers from carrying out everyday maintenance on the course, she asked the Justice Department to provide early warning before workers started major work at the golf course.

Judge Reyes stressed on Monday that she stood by that approach, and she had not tied the government’s hands more than necessary.

“The events surrounding this case have become extraordinary,” she wrote. “The legal result is not.”

During hearings in May and July, she told government lawyers she expected professionalism and that she would trust them to let her know when plans firmed up and if the government was preparing to begin work on the course Mr. Trump had described.

She stressed she would give the Justice Department “the benefit of the doubt” and that she was confident that workers would not “act first and ask forgiveness later.”

But in October, that calculus changed.

“The government then did precisely what plaintiffs feared,” she wrote in an opinion earlier this month.

On a Friday evening, headed into the Columbus Day weekend, the Justice Department filed an update advising that the Interior Department had crafted a plan to clear hundreds of trees across the course. The next morning, just hours later, the crews arrived and cut them down.

At that point, Judge Reyes rebuked the Justice Department, vowing to get answers about who authorized the cutting, whether it was in preparation for Mr. Trump’s renovation and how much time had passed between the decision to cut down the trees and the Justice Department’s filing alerting the court.

In two hearings, she ordered four Interior Department officials to recount how the decision was made. She sparred with Stanley Woodward Jr., the third most senior official at the Justice Department, who stepped in to represent the government.

In the meantime, Mr. Trump announced in several social media posts in October that work would begin “immediately” and the course would close in November to complete the project.

In the opinion on Monday, Judge Reyes wrote that she found the testimony by most of the relatively junior Interior Department officials credible. But she wrote that Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee serving as deputy chief of staff to Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, did not appear to have honestly disclosed what he knew about the plan to remove trees.

She noted that Mr. Wischer had been photographed carrying design plans for the course while touring the grounds with Mr. Trump and Mr. Burgum in June. She expressed doubt that he “just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management,” as he appeared to suggest when describing in court his role managing the course.

item.title: Obama’s ‘Cheesecake Factory’ Jab Rankles Trump on Mississippi Campaign Stop
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama has struck a nerve with President Trump.

Mr. Trump took time from campaign issues to defend his fixation on remodeling the White House in his second term on Monday after Mr. Obama jabbed that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Mr. Trump spoke for several minutes about the remark on his way to a campaign swing in Mississippi, then delivered an extensive aside there on the White House ballroom, helipad and other projects. He was in the solidly Republican state, which has been shifting toward Democrats, as part of his swing through ruby red America to shore up candidates ahead of the midterms.

Mr. Trump, whose approval ratings are at record lows, at times insisted he had spent “very little time” on redesigning the White House, parts of which he has demolished to make way for the new ballroom. But he also defended his focus on the renovations and eventually conceded that “I have fun doing it.”

“It actually relaxes me,” Mr. Trump said in Corinth, asserting he was actually “fixing up the White House.” He added, to cheers from the supportive crowd, “Isn’t that a nice thing to do?”

Even allies and aides inside the White House have conceded that with the war in Iran grinding on, gas prices at uncomfortable highs and Americans chafing at the rising cost of living, Mr. Trump is finding reprieve by focusing on ornate renovation projects in the nation’s capital, chief among them his effort to remake the White House in his image.

Mr. Obama delivered the Cheesecake Factory attack line at a rally in Ohio on Saturday, casting Mr. Trump as out of touch while needling at the president’s extravagant sense of style. Saddam Hussein, the authoritarian leader of Iraq who was ousted by the 2003 U.S. invasion, was known for his love of gold.

The former president’s remarks sparked Mr. Trump’s most devoted critics and supporters. Trump administration officials and other Republicans responded with indignation, and sought to turn the attack upon Mr. Obama. They asserted the former president was the elitist for taking a swing at the Cheesecake Factory. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, had lunch at a Cheesecake Factory in Washington on Monday, quipping “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try.”

No one appeared more insulted than Mr. Trump. In a six-minute gaggle with reporters on his way to Mississippi, the president devoted more than half his speaking time to Mr. Obama’s remarks. He spent comparatively little time repeating his unfounded claims of massive voter fraud.

“For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” Mr. Trump said, before calling Mr. Obama “a stupid person.”

Once onstage, Mr. Trump devoted another six minutes to defending his makeover of the White House, and other parts of the nation’s capital.

“Nobody loved it like I do,” Mr. Trump said of the White House, speaking fondly of beautiful marble and painted columns, and of painstakingly replacing windows and tiles that were in disrepair.

He continued, “We made it all beautiful.”

item.title: A Tight Senate Race in Mississippi? Trump and Others Seem to Think So.
item.description:
Some of the two party’s biggest names, including President Trump and his opponent in 2024, Kamala Harris, have dropped in for rallies. Money is flowing in the millions of dollars. The airwaves are saturated with cutting political ads.

All for a Senate race in Mississippi, one of the most Republican states in the country.

The race between Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, an incumbent Republican, and Scott Colom, a district attorney with deep roots in the state, has raised a tantalizing question in the final days of the midterm season: Could Mississippi, a state flickering on the outskirts of the Democratic Party’s wildest ambitions, actually be in play?

Mr. Trump’s rally on Monday night with Ms. Hyde-Smith in Corinth, a short drive from the Tennessee border, seemed to indicate that it might be.

“I’m here because Cindy is doing great,” the president told the packed arena. “But I’ve just got to make sure.”

He went on to Mr. Colom. “How the hell do you say that guy’s name?” he asked, adding, “I don’t have to go into him — he’s a disaster.”

Mr. Colom seemed happy to take the slight. His campaign posted photos showing him at Mr. Trump’s rally talking to voters in line.

“I hope people will realize that Mississippi was always a state that had potential,” Mr. Colom said this month at a cafe in Jackson, the capital. “But it does need resources and attention.”

In a bastion of conservatism, a healthy dose of skepticism is warranted. Democrats here have let their hopes climb in recent years — with Mike Espy, a former agriculture secretary running for Senate, in 2018, and Brandon Presley, a candidate for governor in 2023 — only to see them dashed.

“We’ve seen this movie before,” Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, said in an interview. “I don’t see the doomsday coming on Nov. 3.”

But the flurry of high-profile surrogates and millions of national dollars from the parties’ official political arms, and their leaderships’ super PACs, signal a tightening race if not a tossup.

“He will never outwork me,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said of Mr. Colom during the rally. “I have a proven record to run on that I am very, very proud of.”

Beyond the rallies and star stand-ins, the money is speaking volumes. Some Black Democrats had clamored for the party establishment to invest in Mississippi and the man who would be the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Mr. Colom, a relentless messenger, has capitalized on boiling voter anger over high prices, cuts to health care and food assistance and the war in Iran.

With the Senate races in Georgia and North Carolina seeming to shift toward the Democrats, Mississippi appears to be the new front in an expanding battlefield in the South.

That prompted a hefty round of spending from the Senate Majority PAC, which is affiliated with the Senate Democratic leadership. The Senate Leadership Fund, connected to Senate Republicans, has now pumped more than $1 million of advertising into Mississippi, according to AdImpact, which monitors campaign advertising,

“Whether he wins or not, he ran a good race,” Mary Wallace Hodge, 79, a retired store manager in Columbus, Miss., said of Mr. Colom. “Republicans are scared.”

Mr. Colom is the son of a barrier-breaking regional judge and a lawyer who worked on Ronald Reagan’s transition team.

Ms. Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the Senate, has not been as dominant as some of her other Republican counterparts. The state’s former agriculture commissioner, Ms. Hyde-Smith was first appointed to the Senate seat after the 2018 retirement of Senator Thad Cochran, who was adept at bringing federal funds to the state.

The state’s senior senator, Roger Wicker, a Republican, has followed in Mr. Cochran’s footsteps as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Ms. Hyde-Smith has a seat on the panel that controls spending and has taken care in recent days to highlight the money that she has driven home. For some Republicans, that is enough to reliably support Mr. Trump’s agenda.

“He can’t do it by himself,” said Sharon Pannell, 57, a retired teacher who came to the rally in Corinth on Monday. “I think a lot of people don’t know how important the midterm election is.”

But Ms. Hyde-Smith has otherwise kept a low profile, declining questions from the reporters who prowl the Senate basement and refusing to debate Mr. Colom. In Starkville, Miss., one farmer told Mr. Colom that he wouldn’t know what Ms. Hyde-Smith looked like, if not for the fairly recent barrage of TV advertisements.

One of her decisions in the Senate was fateful: She refused to sign off on Mr. Colom’s nomination to the federal judiciary during the Biden administration, effectively blocking his path to the lifetime appointment and leaving him free to challenge her this year.

“I wouldn’t have left the bench to run for the United States Senate, that is fair,” Mr. Colom said. But, he said, his motivation was not personal.

“Mississippi did not matter enough to her,” he said. “Ultimately, that’s the betrayal.”

He has pilloried Ms. Hyde-Smith as “Cindy High Prices” and says she has not done enough for the state. He has worked to build a coalition behind the promise that “Mississippi Matters,” playing off a frustration that the state has struggled to climb national rankings.

Then there’s the protein ad.

In February, after a local TV anchor referenced the high price of beef while asking about the rising costs of food, Ms. Hyde-Smith observed: “You have so many proteins to choose from.”

Eight months later, Mr. Colom dropped a punchy, 30-second ad off the clip. A trio of dumbfounded voters riff on the same response: Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator.

It has become the catchphrase on his campaign’s food truck (pick another protein — beef or chicken — for your taco), on campaign posters and even among some voters.

“I’d rather pick another senator,” Kierra Robinson, 33, told Mr. Colom as he knocked on doors in her Jackson neighborhood, quoting the ad back at him in recognition. “I like you.”

An energized Black electorate, which makes up about 40 percent of the state’s population, could lift Mr. Colom but only so far. Former President Barack Obama, whose 2008 campaign prompted a record surge of Black voting, reached about 43 percent that year.

The ongoing effort to redraw districts across the South after the weakening of the Voting Rights Act this year has also helped galvanize many Black voters.

“Mississippi’s not a red state — it’s a state that doesn’t vote,” said Carol Hall, 66, a Southaven, Miss., retiree who had been out canvassing prospective voters for the first time in her life.

But to win, Mr. Colom needs support from more than just Black voters.

Some of those voters seem willing to at least consider him. A young Catholic woman, passionate about her opposition to abortion, said she was looking for a candidate opposed to the data center development near her neighborhood in Horn Lake, Miss., a short drive from Memphis. A gaggle of 18-year-old men spoke about high gas prices and their worries about a protracted conflict in Iran as they debated their first vote.

Roger Keesling said he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but came to Mr. Colom’s rally with Ms. Harris earlier this month to learn more about the guy in the ads that popped up during an episode of “The Voice.”

“I’ve been doing my homework on Cindy Hyde-Smith, and I’m not that impressed,” Mr. Keesling said, speaking before the rally. Mr. Colom, he said, seemed like “he works for the people.”
